prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a real conceptual step. The magic-wavelength trap puts a very large number of neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so Doppler and recoil shifts vanish while quantum projection noise is beaten down by the atom number. Katori proposed this and demonstrated it; Ye's group then took strontium to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and used the clocks to measure gravitational time dilation over centimetre height differences and to bound drifts of constants. That is the kind of result that tells us something about nature, not only about an instrument. It has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST), and these laboratories agree with each other at the 1e-18 level. Seven of the eight opening ballots rank it, five in the top three, and the two-name attribution is the cleanest on our list. It also fits the committee's interest in theory-and-experiment agreement at the highest precision.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness. Hall and Hansch (2005) were honoured for the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable, and Wineland and Haroche (2012) for control of single quantum systems including ion clocks, so a sceptical colleague can call this a successor in a field already prized. Second, the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one can argue the full impact is still to come. Third, Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and others contributed decisive pieces and are outside the two names. I also keep in mind that the field is close to my own, so I may be too fond of it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B042) first as an invention that opens a door, with Rose, Haider and Urban as a natural three-person allocation, while placing B014 second.
responses.response: I take the invention argument seriously, and I agree that a tool can deserve the prize when it opens measurements nobody could make before. But the lattice clock does more than improve resolution: it gave a new physical result, gravitational redshift at the millimetre-to-centimetre scale, and it constrains constants. For B042 I would need the STEM corrector side (Krivanek), which you and Pearce both flag as missing, to be settled. Electron microscopy has also been prized twice already (Ruska 1986 and cryo-EM in 2017). I think B042 is a strong second-tier candidate but not yet cleaner than B014.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B021) first as a detector-driven discovery opening high-energy neutrino astronomy, and puts B014 third, deferring to colleagues on clock priority history.
responses.response: Thank you for deferring on the clocks; I can supply the priority history. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal precedes the strontium lattice demonstrations, and the Ye group's 1e-18 comparisons followed. I do not dispute that IceCube opened a new window, and nature supplied something nobody predicted in detail. My difficulty is attribution and maturity: three names for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers, and source identification that is still thin beyond a few objects. I defer to you and Danielsson on that, but those seem to me larger obstacles than anything in B014.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B014 first because it is the clearest case of a new measurement technique opening new observations, and stresses coherence and linewidth control, but asks whether the committee should wait for the formal redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on coherence and linewidth control, which is exactly why the lattice works. On waiting for the redefinition, I disagree: the prize is for the discovery and its demonstration, which are established and multiply confirmed, not for a metrological decision taken by the CGPM. Waiting risks tying a scientific prize to an administrative schedule. Where I would qualify your view is B008: you pick Cirac, Zoller and Blatt as 'theory plus ions', but Wineland's 2012 prize already covers much of the ion-gate foundation, so I rank it below B014.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B016) first as a new class of states characterised by topology, with a natural theory-plus-experiment trio, and puts B014 fifth.
responses.response: The conceptual originality of topological insulators is not in doubt and I ranked B016 fifth, not last. My reservations are two: the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases, so novelty is arguable, and the credit leaves out the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, which Zhang's death makes impossible to repair, and the 3D work of Fu, Moore and Hasan. As a condensed-matter outsider I cannot weigh this fully, but a trio that omits the proposers of the very system in which the effect was seen seems less safe than the two-name clock award.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B009) first as the natural continuation of the 2025 prize, and discloses his proximity to the field as a possible conflict.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure; it is the right way to handle it. On the science, circuit QED is clean and widely reproduced. My hesitation is timing and narrative: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is only a year old, and Kroll and Eriksson raise the same point. Awarding the next step on the same platform so soon risks looking repetitive, and the allocation among Yale, ETH and Sherbrooke, with Girvin, Majer and others outside the trio, is delicate. I would keep B009 for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Allocation to other early contributors (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others) beyond Katori and Ye.
I have not independently verified exact priority dates or the current record uncertainty values.
If the committee prefers a two-part prize, I would still need a second achievement that fits within a three-person total, and none of the shortlist pairs cleanly with two names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for Katori and Ye; I have no documented collaboration with either. My long-time collaboration with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups concerns a different field. My many-body theory work on atomic structure is close to the clock community, so I flag that proximity for colleagues to weigh my judgement.
